newsitem.title: USA: Chase Manhattan mulls share buyback - CEO.
newsitem.headline: Chase Manhattan mulls share buyback - CEO.

text.p: Chase Manhattan Corp Chairman and Chief Executive Walter Shipley said Thursday a share buy back program is under "active consideration."
"We will continue to return, as we always have, excess capital to our shareholders," he told investors at the Montgomery Securities Conference here.
Shipley said the bank continues to target a baseline return on equity of at least 18 percent, double-digit earnings per share growth and an efficiency ratio in the low 50's.
Shipley declined to address specific earnings projections.
Asked if the bank were on schedule in the operational merger of Chase Manhattan Bank and Chemical Banking Corp, Shipley said on whole the process was ahead of schedule.
"There are literally thousands of goals, so some you're slightly ahead, some you're slightly behind, but in the aggregate we're ahead," he told reporters after the presentation.

Shipley said now, six months after the closing of the merger, executives could for the first time begin to discuss the prospect of capital distribution. He said investors have been inquiring about the bank's intentions.
"A lot of people...are questioning 'What about stock buybacks?'" he said during the presentation. "What I can say about that today is it is under active consideration.

Shipley said management was meeting on the weekend of October 12-13 for a three-day session with outside board directors to review "all the strategies that make up the Chase today" and assess future directions.
He told reporters the high-level meetings could include decisions about further investments or divestitures.

"We will be talking about all the investment opportunities the company has and the redeployment of capital, where appropriate," he said. "The emerging markets broadly continue to be very attractive. We are well positioned there. Asia -- the merger did wonders for us in Asia."

Shipley said in his presentation the bank's businesses were under sharp scrutiny, not only to get over hurdle rates imposed by management but to ensure they provided a "strategic fit" with the bank's overall direction.
"Return is not enough to make the grade," he said.

His presentation centered on the bank's "focused and disciplined strategy for growth" and he said a disciplined commitment to execution was its first, second and third priority to implement its strategy effectively.
"Everything we do is P and L (profit and loss) risk adjusted," he said.
"Those who did not go through the crucible of the 80's, you'd better ask questions," he told investors.

He said Chase's aim was to "leverage our powerful franchise to produce consistent revenue growth: stick to the basics of expense, risk and capital management and develop the major opportunities that are ahead of us."
He said drivers of both its global wholesale and national consumer banking businesses were consistent, based on a relationship orientation and scaling customer franchises.

Shipley said product and market leadership, along the lines of General Electric Co chief Jack Welch, were the bank's top objectives, and managers would need to "figure out a way to get market leadership" to stay in business.

He also discussed the need for one-stop shopping capabilities, and said the bank's information management strategy would be a key asset which only the largest, most powerful banks could afford to develop.
He said the bank has half the number of branches of its three constituent banks five years ago and has eliminated $400 million in expenses to devote resources to technology.

Denis O'Leary, Chase's chief information officer, said outside estimates show Chase's $1.8 billion in 1996 technology spending to be nearly one-third that of the top five banks, who together account for one third all banks' spending.

Shipley noted that all employees had been included in stock options and ownership programs, with strict share ownership requirements for senior management, and he noted share packages were granted at prices of $100 to $120 when the stock was valued at $60 as an ambitious incentive.
"You can see there was a real stretch intent to it but we are confident about the fact that we can get there," he said.
